keyPoints: Big-O describes how running time or memory grows with the input size n, ignoring constant factors.
Common orders from fast to slow: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n).
Worst case is the usual default; best and average cases can differ (for example in quicksort).

questions.question: Which of these grows fastest as n becomes large?
questions.explanation: Quadratic growth overtakes linear, logarithmic and n log n growth for large n.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of reading array[i]?
questions.explanation: The address is computed directly from the index, so it takes constant time.

questions.question: What does O(n) + O(n^2) simplify to?
questions.explanation: Only the fastest-growing term matters in Big-O.

keyPoints: A single loop up to n is O(n); two nested loops each up to n are O(n^2).
A loop that halves or doubles its variable every step runs O(log n) times.
Amortized cost averages expensive rare operations over many cheap ones, for example appending to a dynamic array is O(1) amortized.

questions.question: What is the complexity of a loop over i < n containing a loop over j < n?
questions.explanation: The inner loop runs n times for each of the n outer iterations.

questions.question: How many times does for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) run?
questions.explanation: i doubles each step, so it reaches n after about log2(n) steps.

questions.question: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) solves to...
questions.explanation: There are log n levels and each level does O(n) work, as in merge sort.

keyPoints: Arrays store elements contiguously, so access by index is O(1).
Inserting or deleting in the middle shifts elements, which costs O(n).
Dynamic arrays double their capacity when full, giving amortized O(1) appends.

questions.question: What is the cost of inserting at the start of an array of n elements?
questions.explanation: Every existing element must shift one place to the right.

questions.question: Why is array indexing O(1)?
options: Arrays are always kept sorted by index
Arrays internally use hashing for lookups
Arrays use binary search to find an index
The address is computed from the index directly
questions.explanation: address = start + index * element size.

questions.question: When a dynamic array is full and you append, it typically...
options: Allocates a bigger array and copies the elements
Throws an error until you resize it
Deletes the oldest element to make room
Turns itself into a linked list
questions.explanation: Growing geometrically keeps the amortized cost of append at O(1).

keyPoints: Strings are often immutable, so repeated concatenation in a loop costs O(n^2); use a builder or a list of characters.
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards; check it with two pointers from both ends.
Two strings are anagrams if their character counts match.

questions.question: Best way to check whether s is a palindrome in O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
options: Two pointers moving in from both ends
questions.explanation: Compare s[l] and s[r] while moving l up and r down.

questions.question: How can you check whether two strings are anagrams in O(n)?
options: Sort both and compare in O(1)
questions.explanation: Anagrams have identical counts for every character.

questions.question: Why is s += c in a long loop slow for immutable strings?
options: Each step copies the whole string
questions.explanation: Each += creates a new string and copies all previous characters, giving O(n^2) total.

keyPoints: Two pointers walk an array from both ends or at different speeds, avoiding nested loops.
A sliding window keeps a range [left, right] and updates its sum or counts as it moves, giving O(n).
In a sorted array, move the left pointer up if the sum is too small and the right pointer down if it is too large.

questions.question: Finding a pair that sums to a target in a sorted array with two pointers takes...
questions.explanation: Each step moves one pointer inward, so there are at most n steps.

questions.question: A sliding window is most suited to problems about...
questions.explanation: The window represents a contiguous range that grows and shrinks.

questions.question: In a sorted array, if arr[l] + arr[r] < target, you should...
questions.explanation: The sum is too small, so you need a larger left value.

keyPoints: prefix[i] stores the sum of the first i elements.
The sum of elements l..r is prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l], answered in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.
The same idea works for counts, XOR and 2-D grids.

questions.question: After building prefix sums, a range-sum query costs...
questions.explanation: It is one subtraction of two precomputed values.

questions.question: With prefix[i] = sum of the first i elements, the sum of indexes l..r is...
questions.explanation: prefix[r + 1] covers elements 0..r and prefix[l] covers 0..l-1; the difference is l..r.

questions.question: What does building the prefix array for n elements cost?
questions.explanation: One pass adds each element to the running total.

keyPoints: Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node (and the previous node in a doubly linked list).
Inserting or deleting after a known node is O(1), but finding a node by index is O(n).
Floyd's cycle detection uses a slow and a fast pointer: if they meet, there is a cycle.

questions.question: What is the cost of accessing the i-th node of a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: You must follow next pointers from the head.

questions.question: How does Floyd's algorithm detect a cycle?
options: A slow and a fast pointer eventually meet
questions.explanation: Inside a cycle the fast pointer laps the slow pointer.

questions.question: To reverse a singly linked list in place you...
options: Point each node's next to the previous node
Copy the values into a hash set
questions.explanation: Walk the list while redirecting each next pointer backwards.

keyPoints: A stack is last-in, first-out: push and pop at the top are both O(1).
Stacks check balanced brackets: push openers, and pop and match on closers.
A monotonic stack keeps elements in sorted order to find, for example, the next greater element in O(n).

questions.question: Which order does a stack follow?
questions.explanation: The last element pushed is the first one popped.

questions.question: A stack-based checker processes the string ([)]. What does it report?
options: Only a syntax error at the end
questions.explanation: When ) arrives the top of the stack is [, so the pair does not match.

questions.question: Which structure powers the function call stack?
questions.explanation: Calls return in reverse order of how they were made: last in, first out.

keyPoints: A queue is first-in, first-out: enqueue at the back and dequeue from the front.
A circular buffer reuses array slots with wrap-around indexes: (i + 1) % capacity.
A deque supports insertion and removal at both ends in O(1).

questions.question: Which algorithm is built on a queue?
questions.explanation: BFS visits nodes in the order they were discovered: first in, first out.

questions.question: In a circular array of capacity k, the index after i is...
questions.explanation: The modulo wraps the index back to 0 after k - 1.

questions.question: A deque allows...
options: Insertion and removal at both ends
questions.explanation: Deque means double-ended queue.

keyPoints: A hash function maps a key to an array index; lookups, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average.
Collisions (two keys with the same index) are handled by chaining or open addressing.
Use a map to count frequencies or to find a complement (two-sum) in one pass.

questions.question: What is the average-case lookup time in a hash map?
questions.explanation: The hash jumps almost directly to the right bucket.

questions.question: What is a hash collision?
options: A table that has become completely full
A lookup for a key that is missing
Two keys mapping to the same index
A table whose keys are sorted
questions.explanation: Different keys can produce the same index, so the table needs a collision strategy.

questions.question: Which structure best solves two-sum in O(n)?
options: A hash map from value to index
questions.explanation: For each number, check in O(1) whether target - number was already seen.

keyPoints: Every recursive function needs a base case that stops and a recursive case that moves toward it.
Each call is pushed onto the call stack; a missing base case causes a stack overflow.
Solve the smallest case first, then assume the function already works for smaller inputs.

questions.question: What happens if a recursive function has no reachable base case?
questions.explanation: Calls keep piling up on the call stack until memory runs out.

questions.question: For factorial(n) = n * factorial(n - 1), which is a correct base case?
questions.explanation: 0! = 1 stops the recursion.

questions.question: Where do the local variables of recursive calls live?
questions.explanation: Each call gets its own stack frame.

keyPoints: Binary search needs sorted data and halves the search range each step: O(log n).
Compute the middle as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 to avoid integer overflow.
Binary search on the answer finds the smallest value that satisfies a monotonic condition.

questions.question: Binary search requires the data to be...
questions.explanation: Discarding half the range is only valid when the order is known.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search?
questions.explanation: The range halves each step, so about log2(n) steps.

questions.question: Why write mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2?
options: To avoid overflow of lo + hi
questions.explanation: lo + hi can exceed the int range for very large arrays.

keyPoints: Bubble, selection and insertion sort are O(n^2) in the worst case.
Insertion sort is O(n) on nearly sorted data and is stable.
A stable sort keeps equal elements in their original order; an in-place sort uses O(1) extra space.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time of insertion sort?
questions.explanation: On reverse-sorted input every element moves past all earlier ones.

questions.question: What does 'stable' mean for a sorting algorithm?
options: Equal elements keep their relative order
questions.explanation: Stability matters when sorting records by one key after another.

questions.question: Which elementary sort makes at most n - 1 swaps?
questions.explanation: Selection sort does one swap per pass to place the minimum.

keyPoints: Merge sort splits the array, sorts the halves recursively and merges them: O(n log n) always, O(n) extra space, stable.
Quicksort partitions around a pivot: O(n log n) on average, O(n^2) in the worst case, and it sorts in place.
Both use divide and conquer.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time of quicksort?
questions.explanation: Consistently bad pivots (for example on sorted input with a poor rule) give n levels of O(n) work.

questions.question: Which sort guarantees O(n log n) and is stable?
questions.explanation: Merge sort always splits evenly and its merge step keeps equal elements in order.

questions.question: How much extra space does standard array merge sort need?
questions.explanation: Merging needs a temporary buffer as large as the data.

keyPoints: Backtracking builds a solution step by step and undoes (backtracks) a choice when it cannot lead to a solution.
The template is: choose, explore recursively, un-choose.
Pruning impossible branches early (for example attacked squares in N-Queens) saves time.

questions.question: How many subsets does a set of n distinct elements have?
questions.explanation: Each element is either in or out of a subset, giving 2 choices n times.

questions.question: What is the 'un-choose' step in backtracking for?
options: Sorting the final list of results
Restoring state so other choices can be tried
Freeing memory used by the recursion
questions.explanation: The partial solution must return to its earlier state before trying the next option.

questions.question: How many permutations of n distinct elements are there?
questions.explanation: n choices for the first slot, n-1 for the second, and so on.

keyPoints: A binary tree node has at most two children; the top node is the root and nodes without children are leaves.
Pre-order visits root, left, right; in-order visits left, root, right; post-order visits left, right, root.
Level-order traversal uses a queue and visits nodes level by level.

questions.question: Which traversal visits left subtree, then root, then right subtree?
questions.explanation: In-order puts the root between its two subtrees.

questions.question: Which data structure drives level-order traversal?
questions.explanation: A queue processes nodes in the order they were discovered, level by level.

questions.question: What is a leaf node?
questions.explanation: Leaves are the nodes at the bottom with no children.

keyPoints: In a BST every value in the left subtree is smaller and every value in the right subtree is larger than the node.
Search, insert and delete take O(h), where h is the height: O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if skewed.
In-order traversal of a BST visits the values in sorted order.

questions.question: In-order traversal of a BST yields the values...
questions.explanation: Left (smaller), node, right (larger) visits values in ascending order.

questions.question: What is the worst-case search time in an unbalanced BST?
questions.explanation: A skewed tree is a chain, so search may visit every node.

questions.question: Inserting 5, then 3, then 8 into an empty BST: where does 3 go?
questions.explanation: 3 < 5, so it becomes the left child of the root 5.

keyPoints: A binary heap is a complete tree stored in an array where each parent is <= (min-heap) or >= (max-heap) its children.
Insert and remove-top are O(log n); peeking at the top is O(1); building a heap from n items is O(n).
A priority queue is usually a heap; keep a min-heap of size k to find the k largest elements.

questions.question: What is the time to read the minimum of a min-heap?
questions.explanation: The minimum is always at the root.

questions.question: Which structure usually implements a priority queue?
questions.explanation: A heap supports insert and extract-min in O(log n).

questions.question: To find the k largest elements of a stream, a good approach is...
questions.explanation: The heap keeps the k largest seen so far; its root is the smallest of them and gets evicted first.

keyPoints: A trie stores strings character by character along paths from the root.
Insert, search and prefix checks cost O(L), where L is the word length, regardless of how many words are stored.
Tries power autocomplete and prefix search.

questions.question: What is the time to look up a word of length L in a trie?
questions.explanation: You follow one node per character.

questions.question: Tries are especially good for...
questions.explanation: All words with a common prefix share the same path from the root.

questions.question: How does a trie mark the end of a stored word?
options: An end-of-word flag on the node
Storing the word length at the root
questions.explanation: The path alone cannot tell a stored word from a prefix, so the node carries a flag.

keyPoints: Inserting sorted data into a plain BST creates a skewed tree with O(n) operations.
Balanced trees (AVL, red-black) keep the height O(log n) using rotations.
AVL trees are more strictly balanced; red-black trees do fewer rotations and are used in, for example, Java's TreeMap.

questions.question: Why can a plain BST become slow?
options: Inserting sorted data makes it a chain
questions.explanation: Each new value goes to the same side, so the height becomes n.

questions.question: Which operation restores balance in an AVL tree?
questions.explanation: Rotations rearrange nodes locally to reduce the height.

questions.question: Which Java collection is backed by a red-black tree?
questions.explanation: TreeMap keeps keys sorted using a red-black tree.

keyPoints: A graph has vertices (nodes) and edges; edges may be directed or undirected and may carry weights.
An adjacency list stores each vertex's neighbours: O(V + E) space, good for sparse graphs.
An adjacency matrix uses O(V^2) space but checks whether an edge u-v exists in O(1).

questions.question: How much space does an adjacency list use?
questions.explanation: One list entry per vertex plus one entry per edge.

questions.question: Which representation checks whether an edge exists in O(1)?
questions.explanation: matrix[u][v] is a direct array lookup.

questions.question: A graph with far fewer edges than V^2 is called...
questions.explanation: Sparse graphs are best stored as adjacency lists.

keyPoints: BFS explores level by level using a queue; DFS goes deep first using recursion or a stack.
Both run in O(V + E) with an adjacency list and need a visited set to avoid looping.
BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS is useful for connected components and cycle detection.

questions.question: Which finds the path with the fewest edges in an unweighted graph?
questions.explanation: BFS reaches every vertex in order of distance from the start.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of BFS on an adjacency list?
questions.explanation: Each vertex and each edge is processed once.

questions.question: Why keep a visited set in graph traversal?
options: To avoid revisiting nodes and looping forever
questions.explanation: Graphs can contain cycles, so without it the traversal may never end.

keyPoints: A topological order lists the vertices of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so that every edge goes from an earlier to a later vertex.
Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes vertices with in-degree 0 using a queue.
If not all vertices get removed, the graph contains a cycle.

questions.question: A topological ordering exists only for...
questions.explanation: A cycle would require some vertex to come before itself.

questions.question: Kahn's algorithm starts with the vertices that have...
questions.explanation: Vertices with no incoming edges have no prerequisites and can come first.

questions.question: Kahn's algorithm processes fewer than V vertices. What does that mean?
questions.explanation: Vertices on a cycle never reach in-degree 0.

keyPoints: BFS gives shortest paths when all edges have the same weight.
Dijkstra's algorithm uses a min-priority queue and repeatedly settles the closest unsettled vertex; it needs non-negative weights.
Dijkstra runs in O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap.

questions.question: Dijkstra's algorithm requires edge weights to be...
questions.explanation: A negative edge could make an already settled vertex reachable more cheaply.

questions.question: Which data structure makes Dijkstra's algorithm efficient?
questions.explanation: It picks the unsettled vertex with the smallest distance in O(log V).

questions.question: The shortest path in an unweighted graph is best found with...
questions.explanation: BFS is linear time and needs no priority queue.

keyPoints: A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices of a weighted undirected graph with minimum total weight and no cycles.
Kruskal's algorithm sorts the edges and adds the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle, using union-find.
Union-find supports find and union in nearly O(1) with path compression and union by rank.

questions.question: How many edges does an MST of a connected graph with V vertices have?
questions.explanation: A tree on V vertices has exactly V - 1 edges.

questions.question: Which structure detects cycles in Kruskal's algorithm?
questions.explanation: If two endpoints are already in the same set, adding the edge would create a cycle.

questions.question: What does Kruskal's algorithm do first?
options: Builds a heap of all vertices
questions.explanation: It considers edges from cheapest to most expensive.

keyPoints: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders.
Interval scheduling: sort by end time and pick each interval that starts after the last chosen one ends.
Greedy fails for problems such as coin change with arbitrary coin values; use dynamic programming there.

questions.question: To select the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals greedily, sort by...
questions.explanation: Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the remaining intervals.

questions.question: With coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6, greedy picks 4 + 1 + 1. What is the optimal number of coins?
questions.explanation: 3 + 3 uses two coins, so greedy is not optimal here.

questions.question: A greedy algorithm is guaranteed correct when...
questions.explanation: The locally best choice must always be part of some optimal solution.

keyPoints: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.
Memoization is top-down: cache the results of recursive calls. Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table in order.
Naive Fibonacci recursion is exponential; dynamic programming makes it O(n).

questions.question: What does memoization mean?
questions.explanation: Each subproblem is solved once and its answer is reused.

questions.question: Naive recursive Fibonacci runs in about...
questions.explanation: The same values are recomputed over and over, so the call tree grows exponentially.

questions.question: Bottom-up DP fills its table...
options: From the base cases upward to the answer
questions.explanation: Each entry depends only on entries that were already filled.

keyPoints: Define dp[i] clearly, for example the best answer using the first i items.
Climbing stairs: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]. House robber: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]).
Coin change: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - coin]) over the coins; the standard LIS dynamic program is O(n^2).

questions.question: Climbing stairs with steps of 1 or 2: how many ways to reach step 4?
questions.explanation: ways(1)=1, ways(2)=2, ways(3)=3, ways(4)=5: each is the sum of the previous two.

questions.question: What is the house robber recurrence for dp[i]?
questions.explanation: Either skip house i, or rob it and add the best from two houses back.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the coin change DP for amount A and n coins?
questions.explanation: For each amount up to A it tries each of the n coins.

keyPoints: A 2-D table such as dp[i][j] often indexes prefixes of two strings or positions in a grid.
LCS: if the characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; otherwise max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
0/1 knapsack: dp[i][w] = max(skip item i, take item i if it fits); edit distance takes the minimum of insert, delete and replace.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of LCS for strings of lengths m and n?
questions.explanation: The table has m * n cells and each takes constant time.

questions.question: In 0/1 knapsack, each item can be used...
questions.explanation: 0/1 means each item is either taken or left.

questions.question: Which operations does edit distance allow?
questions.explanation: The edit distance is the minimum number of insertions, deletions and replacements.
